title: What Stopped the Pump
logline: A customer brings in a water pump that 'just stopped'. The repairer opens the casing, and what looked like one broken thing turns out to be several small failures that only add up once you look closely.

object.note: Object 9 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject. Object 3, marked by conflict and repair, may also recur beside another thing opened up to find its causes.

thread_in.thread: The water that starts the chain meets a machine that stopped: a repairer opening a water pump to find not one cause but several small ones.

thread_out.thread: From causes found inside one machine to a chain spread across one day: a fish netted at dawn on the west coast and eaten inland by nightfall.

requirements: An established small-appliance or vehicle repair shop willing to be filmed over real working days
At least two or three genuine repair jobs within the filming window
A repairer willing to explain their diagnosis on camera

suggestions.name: A small market town with an established repair trade
suggestions.region: Vavuniya or Kilinochchi district, Northern Province
suggestions.why: Gives the group a northern setting distinct from its other locations, and small-town repair shops are common along the main market roads there.
suggestions.verify: A specific shop and repairer must be identified and confirmed.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: When something breaks, the one-line reason ('it just stopped') is true, but so is the long list of small things that together made it stop. You need both answers to really understand it.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: යමක් නැවතුණු විට 'ඉබේම නැවතුණා' යන කෙටි පිළිතුරත්, ඒ පිටුපස ඇති කුඩා හේතු රැසේ දිගු පිළිතුරත් යන දෙකම ඇත්ත වන අතර, හොඳින් තේරුම් ගන්නට දෙකම අවශ්‍යය.
lesson.the_teaching: The texts begin the study of conditions by asking whether mind and matter arise by themselves or are made by some powerful being, and answer that they arise from many causes. Both books say the Buddha taught cause and effect at three lengths: very briefly, at middle length as dependent origination, which names only one principal cause at each step, and in full detail as the Paṭṭhāna's twenty-four conditions. Margaya says the first tells us that one thing arises because of another, the second tells us through which powers and in which ways, and both are needed for complete understanding. It adds that there is nothing that is not a condition for something.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The customer's one-line account of the fault opens the film; then the casing comes off and the parts are laid out, tested one by one and named, and a worn part is traced back to what it depended on. The distance between the short story told at the counter and the long, exact one told by the repairer's hands is where the viewer finds the lesson, whether the pump runs again or the repairer honestly says it cannot be fixed.

key_terms.en: dependent origination, the middle-length account (one main cause per step)
the detailed account: twenty-four kinds of support

lesson.caution: It does not mean 'everything happens for a reason': a condition is not a purpose or a plan, the texts rule out a maker, and the machine is only an everyday picture, not the teaching itself.
lesson.builds_on: The last film showed many supports holding up one harvest; this one turns the lens round and shows that when something stops, many small conditions stand behind that too.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
